# Nandakovāda Sutta (MN 146 (PTS MN iii 270))
**ID:** MN 146 (PTS MN iii 270)

**Title (Pali):** Nandakovāda Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Advice from Nandaka

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Nandakovāda Sutta* ("Advice from Nandaka", MN 146) is set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The narrative begins when Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approaches the Buddha accompanied by five hundred nuns to request Dhamma instruction [Anālayo 2010; Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Although the monk Nandaka had previously been avoiding his assigned turn to instruct the nuns, the Buddha specifically directs him to teach them, addressing him with high regard as "brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) [Anālayo 2016; Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. Nandaka structures his discourse as an interactive catechism, explicitly inviting the nuns to engage, respond, and ask for further explanation if needed [SuttaCentral; Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. He leads them through a detailed examination of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*) across the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and their corresponding types of consciousness [Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Rogell 2003]. To explain how passion binds the faculties, Nandaka presents a sequence of allegories: comparing the external bases to a great tree, and likening the internal and external faculties to the flesh and hide of a cow bound by inner sinews and tendons (representing desire and lust), which are severed by the sharp butcher's knife of noble wisdom [Kuznetsova et al. 2012].
Comparative analysis by Bhikkhu Anālayo highlights that in the Pali version, the Buddha does not directly address or teach Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, unlike several non-Theravāda parallel accounts where he teaches her personally; Anālayo identifies this feature as part of a later redactional tendency toward narrative distancing of nuns within the Theravāda tradition [Anālayo 2010; Anālayo 2011; Anālayo 2016]. Curated parallels include a discourse in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 276 / T 99), Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 68 and 85), Tibetan Kangyur translations (D 3 and D 4106), and a Sarvāstivāda/Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya version (T 1442.30) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates extensive cross-linguistic alignment with the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) and the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D 3), while also identifying machine matches with the *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D 4094), *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and *Śroṇasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali Canon, DharmaNexus reveals extensive textual reuse with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 147), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Diṭṭhi Saṁyutta* (SN 24), and *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1) [DharmaNexus]. The sutta is also cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 13.8) [SuttaCentral].
